title: The ACL decision space
summary: Five ways to keep unreadable chunks away from a caller: post-filter, pre-filter, physical isolation, live source check and delegation to the source. Four dials choose among them.
useIf: You must pick where document permissions are enforced and want to see how the choice flips.
avoidIf: You already know the mechanism and need its details. Open the topic for that option.

explain.md: Every option answers two questions: **which component decides**, and **which stages see text the caller may not read**. A post-filter lets denied text reach your code, rerankers, logs and caches. A pre-filter keeps it inside the index. Four dials choose among the options: the **permission model** (one tag, groups, rich per-document rules), **revocation speed**, **tenancy** and **scale** (how much of the corpus a caller may see).

explain.md: Tier the data before you choose. Public and low-impact content can use the cheapest option, while a restricted tier may need a live check or a physical wall. Pick the option per tier, state the revocation target for each, and test it with a revoked canary user. Most real systems then combine two options: a pre-filter for the bulk of traffic and a live check on the top hits of restricted tiers. That pairing is design reasoning from the sources, not a vendor prescription.

explain.title: Rank the ACL options
explain.prompt: Flip the three dials. The ranking and the reason for each cell update.

options.name: Post-filter
options.summary: Retrieve top-k, then drop what the caller cannot read.

options.name: Pre-filter in the index
options.summary: Security filter (GA) or native ACLs (preview), applied before ranking.

options.name: Pre-filter plus live check
options.summary: Filter in the index, then verify the top hits at the source.

options.name: Delegate to the source
options.summary: The system of record retrieves with the caller's token.

group.why: A few percent visible starves recall.

rich.why: Any rule fits in code, top-k is still wasted.

hours.why: Same lag as any ACL copy.

minutes.why: No fresher than the ACL data it reads.

seconds.why: Needs a live lookup per hit.

few.why: Thin slice of a big corpus.

group.why: search.in over group ids, before ranking.

rich.why: Deny rules must flatten to allow lists.

minutes.why: Needs frequent pushes or short runs.

seconds.why: Only with push merge and an event feed.

few.why: Works, big tenants may want a wall.

tag.why: Nothing to verify beyond the tag.

rich.why: Source decides on the hits that matter.

hours.why: Latency for freshness you do not need.

minutes.why: Checked hits live, the rest age.

seconds.why: Live for what the user sees.

few.why: A few parallel checks are affordable.

huge.why: Budget rate limits and the tail.

tag.why: Your own index can filter a tag.
Physical boundary, no filter to forget.

group.why: Nothing for groups inside a tenant.

rich.why: Per-document rules still need a filter.

minutes.why: Same as the filter inside the tenant.

explain.takeaway: No option wins every dial. Pre-filter wins the common group-based case, a live check buys seconds-level revocation, and a wall buys isolation at a cost in scale.

explain.intro: Compare post-filter, pre-filter, pre-filter plus live check and a per-tenant index on recall, latency and leakage. Start with the group-based preset, then run the three guided experiments.

explain.title: Preview status, checked 2026-10-13
explain.md: Only security filters are GA. Native ACL and RBAC scopes, Purview labels and SharePoint ACLs need a preview API, carry no SLA and are not recommended for production by the docs [[r11]].

pitfalls.symptom: Median users get one result instead of ten
pitfalls.cause: A post-filter starves top-k at a visible fraction of a few percent
pitfalls.fix: Filter inside the index, or over-fetch by about 1 divided by the visible fraction and monitor recall

pitfalls.symptom: A revoked user still sees a document
pitfalls.cause: The ACL copy is older than the change, or a cache holds the answer
pitfalls.fix: State a target per tier, shorten sync for restricted data, scope caches by ACL

pitfalls.symptom: One choice was made for the whole corpus
pitfalls.cause: Dials were not stated per sensitivity tier
pitfalls.fix: Tier the data, then pair a pre-filter with a live check for the restricted tier

scenarios.title: Broad wiki on a fixed search service
scenarios.situation: An assistant covers a wiki where about 90% of pages are visible to everyone. Another team manages the search service and it cannot store ACL fields. An entitlement service answers who may read a page. Hourly staleness is fine.
unknowns: How many pages per query need an entitlement lookup?
Do candidates reach logs or a reranker first?
scenarios.question: Where do you enforce permissions?

options.name: Pre-filter after a re-ingest that adds ACL fields
options.why: It is the better long-term design.
options.tradeoff: Needs a schema change you do not control today.

options.name: Post-filter with about 1.3 times over-fetch, before reranking and logging, with a recall check
options.why: Almost everything is visible, so top-k barely shrinks and no schema change is needed.
options.tradeoff: Denied text still reaches your code, so keep it out of logs and caches.

options.name: One index per user
options.why: Thousands of users exceed index caps (200 on S2 and S3) and multiply cost [[r20]].
options.tradeoff: Only sensible for a handful of principals.

flips.if: The visible fraction drops to 5% or lower
flips.then: Post-filter starves top-k. Move the filter into the index.
Add a security filter and keep the entitlement check for sensitive pages.

scenarios.takeaway: Post-filtering is acceptable when almost everything is visible and the index cannot filter.

scenarios.title: Thousands of small tenants
scenarios.situation: A SaaS product serves 4,000 tenants, each with a few thousand documents. Contracts require logical separation and deletion within thirty days. Members of a tenant share one permission level.
unknowns: Is physical separation required by regulation?
Can every query go through one gateway?
scenarios.question: Which isolation model do you choose?

options.name: Service per tenant
options.why: Four thousand services multiply cost and operations.
options.tradeoff: Right for a few regulated tenants.

options.name: Index per tenant on a high-density tier
options.tradeoff: S3 HD allows 1,000 indexes per partition or 3,000 per service, so 4,000 needs a second service [[r20]].

options.name: Shared index, with a gateway injecting the tenant filter from the authenticated identity
options.why: It scales to thousands of tenants with one operating model [[r22]].
options.tradeoff: One missed filter exposes every tenant, so test with a canary tenant and block direct index access.

flips.if: Three tenants are 100 times larger and regulated
flips.then: Give those their own service and keep the rest shared.
A wall per tenant becomes mandatory and cost follows.

scenarios.takeaway: Many small tenants favour a shared index with an enforced filter.

scenarios.title: Per-document rules, seconds-level revocation
scenarios.situation: Content sits in a document system with per-item permissions, deny rules and sharing links. Security requires a revoked grant to stop working within seconds. Answers cite up to eight documents.
unknowns: What request rate and latency does the source API allow?
What happens when the source is down?
scenarios.question: Which design fits?

options.name: Delegate retrieval to the source with the caller's token
options.why: Always current, and the source applies its own rules.
options.tradeoff: Little ranking control and quotas, such as 200 requests per user per hour for the Copilot Retrieval API [[r26]].

options.name: Pre-filter only, with a nightly indexer
options.why: Deny rules are hard to flatten and a nightly sync cannot meet seconds.
options.tradeoff: Right when permissions are groups and a day of lag is fine.

options.name: Pre-filter for recall, then a parallel live check on the top hits, failing closed on timeout
options.why: The source decides on the few documents the user will see, so revocation is live where it counts.
options.tradeoff: A latency tail and source load, and a slow source hides documents.

flips.if: Revocation relaxes to a few hours
flips.then: Drop the live check and rely on the pre-filter.

flips.if: The content already lives in a store with a permission-aware retrieval API

scenarios.takeaway: Live checks buy seconds-level revocation for rich rules.

quiz.q: Revocation must take effect within seconds for per-document rules stored in a source system. Which option moves up?
options: A live check on the top hits, or delegating retrieval to the source
quiz.explain: Only a live decision at the source reflects a change in seconds. A nightly sync and a post-filter over copied ACLs inherit the copy's age, and an index per user does not solve per-document rules.

quiz.q: Match each option to its main limit.

pairs.r: Top-k fills with denied hits when access is selective
Lag between a source change and the index
Index caps and operations cost at thousands of tenants
Little ranking control and per-user rate limits

quiz.explain: Each option fails where its mechanism is weakest: post-filtering at low visible fractions, a pre-filter at sync lag, a wall at tenant count, delegation at control and quota.
